## SCENE 01: Hook
image: s01_endless_thumb
prompt: Bob slumps on a doodle couch with a glowing phone in one hand, thumb mid-swipe, looking bored and sleepy. A tiny wall clock behind him shows very late at night. Plain white background, 16:9.
music: none

### Narration
(deadpan) {cam:zoom_in|8} In the next eight minutes, I'll explain why you can't stop scrolling, {text:3 FIXES|pop} and hand you three fixes for tonight.
[pause]
(flat) But first, a question. {img:sarcastic_wow|2.5} You didn't even like that stranger's kitchen renovation, so why did you watch {text:FORTY MINUTES|slam} all forty minutes?
(smug) Here's the secret. {sfx:pizzicato_sting} It isn't weak willpower. [pause:short] It's engineering.
(deadpan) Somewhere, smart people got paid well to make sure you {text:NO BOTTOM|slam} never reach the bottom.
(flat) Don't worry. {text:IT ENDS|pop} This video has a bottom. [pause:beat] I checked.
(smug) {cam:punch_in} First, the thing the feed quietly took away from you.

## SCENE 02: No Exit
image: s02_no_ending
prompt: Bob stands beside a long doodle scroll of blank rectangles unrolling endlessly off the right edge of the frame, holding a blank paper sign and shrugging. Plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(deadpan) Think about how things used to end. {text:ENDINGS|fade} A newspaper had a last page. A show had credits. A book had a back cover.
(flat) Those were stopping cues. Quiet little signals that said, "Okay, you're done." {cam:punch_in} Your brain leans on them more than you'd think.
(smug) The feed removed the signal. {sfx:whoosh} New posts load on their own, forever, so there's never a page to turn.
[pause]
(deadpan) So the question quietly changes. {text:WHY STOP?|pop} It stops being "should I keep going," and becomes "why would I stop?"
(flat) {img:done_with_everything|2.5} And at eleven PM, nobody has a good answer.
(fake fancy) Imagine a buffet that refills itself while you chew. {text:INFINITE BUFFET|slam} Elegant. Sophisticated. Slightly unwise.
(flat) Normally your stomach says stop. Scrolling has no stomach. {sfx:bonk} It has a thumb, and the thumb has no opinions.
(deadpan) Meanwhile, the kitchen renovation just auto-played {text:EPISODE ELEVEN|jitter} episode eleven. I did not ask for episode eleven. [pause:beat] I'm watching episode eleven.
(smug) {cam:pan_left|6} But a missing exit is only half the trap. The other half is a reward you can never predict.

## SCENE 03: The Lever
image: s03_lever
prompt: Bob sits at a big doodle slot machine and pulls its lever with one hand, a glowing phone screen where the reels would be. A tiny dog photo and a few coins hang in the air. Plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(deadpan) {cam:zoom_in|6} Last century, a psychologist named Skinner studied how animals respond to rewards. {text:SKINNER|pop} One pattern kept them pressing a lever remarkably hard.
(flat) Not a steady reward. An unpredictable one. [pause:short] Sometimes a treat, sometimes nothing, and no way to know which press pays.
(smug) Researchers call it a variable reward. Casinos call it {sfx:ka_ching} a business model.
[pause]
(deadpan) Now apply it. You swipe down. {sfx:whoosh} Most of the time, you get {text:BORING|shrink} a stranger's lunch.
(dramatic) Then, out of nowhere, a perfect {sfx:angelic_chime}{text:JACKPOT|slam} dog video.
(flat) Your brain notes that, and files a rule. [pause:short] {cam:punch_in} Check the next one. The next one might be the dog.
(deadpan) {img:fourth_wall|2.5} Here's the honest caveat. Those experiments were on animals. Humans are messier, so "slot machine" is an analogy, not a lab result.
(flat) {text:AN ANALOGY|fade} Still, it's a decent analogy. You pull, you wait, you might win. You just pay in minutes instead of coins.
(smug) And the jackpot, for some reason, keeps turning out to be terrible news. Let's talk about that.

## SCENE 04: Smoke Detector
image: s04_smoke_detector
prompt: Bob stands under a giant doodle smoke detector blaring with wavy lines, holding a slice of toast with a flat, unimpressed look. Small cards float around him: a rain cloud, a gossip speech bubble, a flame. Plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(deadpan) Psychologists call it {text:NEGATIVITY BIAS|slam} negativity bias. The idea is that bad information tends to get more weight than good information.
(flat) Rozin and Royzman wrote a well-known review of it in two thousand one. {cam:punch_in} It holds up well, though researchers still argue about the details.
(deadpan) The usual explanation is evolutionary. The ancestors who ignored the rustling {text:BUSH LUNCH|pop} bush became the bush's lunch.
(smug) So your brain is a smoke detector. Extremely sensitive. [pause:short] Cannot tell a fire from {text:IT'S TOAST|jitter} toast.
(flat) Now add a feed that sorts by what keeps you looking. [pause] A calm update about the weather? {text:SUNNY, PROBABLY|shrink} Skip.
(dramatic) A celebrity feud with three new twists? {sfx:drum_roll} {text:STAY FOREVER|slam} Stay forever.
(flat) That's the doom in doomscrolling. You're not hunting for bad news. {cam:punch_in} Your brain is good at noticing it, and the feed noticed that you noticed.
(whisper) Which means the real culprit might not be you at all.
[pause:long]

## SCENE 05: Not a Flaw
image: s05_not_a_flaw
prompt: Bob studies a doodle blueprint of a feed marked with simple icons: an endless arrow, a lever, a siren. He nods slowly like a mechanic inspecting an engine. A small magnifying glass hovers beside him. Plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(deadpan) {cam:zoom_out|6} "Just one more" feels like a decision. It isn't, really. It's the product doing its job. {text:NOT A FLAW|slam}
(flat) No finish line, a reward you can't predict, and a brain that leans toward bad news. That's a design feature, not a defect in you.
(smug) {sfx:triumphant_sting} Congratulations. You're a perfectly normal human using a perfectly engineered habit machine.
(flat) Now, honesty time. {text:BE HONEST|pop} Studies often link heavy news scrolling with a worse mood.
(deadpan) But most of that research is correlational. {text:CORRELATION|fade} It shows two things move together, not that one causes the other. Feeling worse might make you scroll more, too.
(flat) {img:done_with_everything|2.5} So I can't promise that quitting fixes your mood. I'm a cartoon, not a doctor.
(deadpan) If it's weighing on you, a real professional is a better bet than me. {cam:punch_in} What I can do is make the habit less sticky.
(flat) Low effort only, because {text:CAN'T BE BOTHERED|pop} I can't be bothered. [pause:short] Three fixes. One for the exit, one for the lever, one for the bad news.
(smug) Starting with the exit.

## SCENE 06: Timer and Charger
image: s06_timer_and_charger
prompt: Split layout. On the left, Bob holds up a kitchen timer with a smug look. On the right, a phone sits plugged into a wall charger at the far end of a long doodle hallway while Bob stares at it from the couch. Plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(deadpan) {text:FIX ONE|slam} Fix one. Give the feed an ending. Set a timer before you open it. Ten minutes, say.
(flat) When it rings, that's your bottom. {sfx:phone_ring} It's a homemade stopping cue. Not perfect. Beats nothing.
(smug) And yes, you'll ignore it the first time. [pause:short] That's allowed. {text:STILL COUNTS|pop} Noticing you ignored it is half the trick.
[pause]
(deadpan) Fix two, for the lever. {text:ADD FRICTION|slam} Add friction. Charge your phone across the room, not next to your bed.
(flat) Habits love effortless. {cam:punch_in} Make the lever a little harder to reach, and the automatic part tends to wobble.
(smug) Now you have to stand up, walk over, and make an {text:ACTUAL DECISION|jitter} actual decision. Which is exactly what the feed was avoiding.
(deadpan) For most of us, standing up is the longest distance in the house. {sfx:sad_trombone}
(smug) {img:smug_genius|2.5} Yes, it's annoying. That's the point. Annoying is a speed bump, and speed bumps are legal.
(flat) Last fix is for the bad news. It's also the nicest one.

## SCENE 07: The Reveal
image: s07_reveal
prompt: Bob sits on a doodle couch holding a plain paper book, relaxed and unbothered. A small framed doodle of a tidy finished kitchen hangs on the wall behind him. Otherwise plain white background, 16:9.

### Narration
(deadpan) {text:FINISH LINE|slam} Fix three. Swap the slot machine for something with an ending. An episode. A chapter. A crossword. A puzzle with a last square.
(flat) You still get a small reward, but the thing actually stops, and you get to feel finished. {sfx:ta_da} Wild concept. Stuff that finishes.
(deadpan) Tonight, try one. Timer, charger, or something with an ending. {text:TRY ONE|pop} You don't need all three. I couldn't be bothered either.
[pause]
(deadpan) Remember that stranger's kitchen renovation? {img:sarcastic_wow|2} I'll tell you what it had. A final reveal. Cabinets, countertops, a very proud person wiping a very clean counter.
(flat) It ended. Good things usually do. The feed just won't be the one to tell you.
[pause:long]
(deadpan) The kitchen got a finish line. You can have one too.
